brief.question: What were the main debates in the Australian parliament in 2008, and what positions did members and parties take? Debates that year included The Apology, The global financial crisis, Grocery and fuel bills and The alcopops tax.
brief.answer:
The Australian Parliament’s 2008 sittings were dominated by the global financial crisis and the government’s response to it. The Rudd government introduced an Economic Security Strategy, a $10.4 billion package of bills providing $4.8 billion in payments to pensioners, carers, senior health card holders and veterans, $3.9 billion for families, $1.5 billion for first home buyers, and $187 million for training. Government speakers argued the package was a swift, targeted and prudent response to a dramatic shift in Australia’s macroeconomic outlook, with payments to begin from 8 December 2008. Opposition members criticised the package and the government’s broader handling of the crisis, with one coalition speaker accusing the Prime Minister of declaring “war” on inflation, unemployment and other issues without delivering results, noting inflation had risen every quarter since the declaration. The same speaker argued the government’s bank guarantee announcements had dislocated the market, and that unemployment was projected to rise to nearly six per cent, with around 270,000 Australians having had their assets frozen.

The opposition also sought to force a debate on the crisis, with the House of Representatives voting 71 to 55 on 12 November 2008 to call on the business of the day for that debate. Government members accused the coalition of inconsistency, with one minister describing a “litany of different positions” from the opposition leader on the economic strategy, while another government senator said the opposition had spent time blocking budget bills earlier in the year. The government also noted the crisis had forced a downward revision of revenue by some $40 billion over the years 2008-09 to 2011-12, and that the budget surplus was reduced as a result. The debate extended to related legislation, including the Nation-building Funds Bill 2008, which established funds for infrastructure investment to address both immediate challenges from the crisis and longer-term needs.
